title: Kata Containers, gVisor or Firecracker?

rows.label: In one line
values: Containers that each get their own small VM
Containers that talk to a user-space kernel instead of the host’s
A tiny VM monitor that other platforms build sandboxes on

rows.label: What it is
values: An OCI runtime that boots a VM per pod, using QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker or the built-in Dragonball
An application kernel written in Go (the Sentry) plus `runsc`, an OCI runtime
A virtual machine monitor in Rust: one process runs one microVM, configured through a REST API

rows.label: Isolation boundary
values: Hardware virtualisation: a separate guest kernel for each pod
Software: the Sentry serves system calls itself and runs under a seccomp filter; no hardware boundary
Hardware virtualisation: a separate guest kernel per microVM, with the `jailer` sandboxing the monitor process

rows.label: Where it plugs in
values: containerd or CRI-O as the shim v2 runtime `containerd-shim-kata-v2`; Docker with `--runtime io.containerd.kata.v2`
Docker with `--runtime=runsc`; containerd through `containerd-shim-runsc-v1`; CRI-O
Your own code, over the API socket; containers only through Kata or firecracker-containerd

rows.label: Kubernetes
values: Yes, as a `RuntimeClass`; managed in AKS Pod Sandboxing and GKE Sandbox microVMs
Yes, as a `RuntimeClass` named `gvisor`; managed in GKE Sandbox, on by default in Autopilot
Not by itself: only underneath Kata or another runtime

rows.label: Host requirements
values: Linux with KVM: bare metal, or VMs with nested virtualisation
Any Linux host, including cloud VMs without nested virtualisation; the KVM platform is faster on bare metal
Linux with KVM; on EC2 that means `.metal` instances

rows.label: Start-up and overhead
values: On GKE (with Cloud Hypervisor): about 1 to 2 s to start and a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod
On GKE: under 200 ms to start and memory that grows with the app, but every system call costs more than on Linux
Under 125 ms to boot and under 5 MiB of overhead; up to 150 microVMs per second on one host

rows.label: Compatibility
values: A real Linux kernel inside, so almost anything runs; gaps are at the VM edge, such as no host networking or `subPath` mounts
290 of 352 amd64 system calls and not every `/proc` or `/sys` file; no privileged containers on GKE
Linux guests (and OSv) with a handful of virtio devices; you supply the kernel and root filesystem

rows.label: GPUs
values: Yes, with QEMU, which also supports confidential computing (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP)
Some NVIDIA GPUs through `nvproxy`; specific GPUs and TPUs on GKE
No: device passthrough (VFIO) is still an open feature request

rows.label: Who runs it in production
values: Azure (AKS Pod Sandboxing), Google (GKE Sandbox microVMs), Baidu
Google (GKE Sandbox, Cloud Run first generation, App Engine), Ant Group, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cloudflare
AWS Lambda, Fly.io Machines, E2B sandboxes

tip: These aren’t three rival products. Firecracker is a building block, and Kata can use it as its hypervisor, so “Kata or Firecracker” is often “Kata with Firecracker”. The real choice is the boundary: a VM with its own kernel (Kata on any hypervisor, or Firecracker under a platform you build yourself) or gVisor’s user-space kernel. Pick gVisor when your nodes have no KVM, or when start-up time and density matter and your software fits its system-call coverage. Pick Kata when you need a full Linux kernel, privileged containers or GPUs, and can run on bare metal or nested virtualisation. Use Firecracker directly only if you’re building your own sandbox or functions platform and are ready to supply the kernel, root filesystem, networking and scheduler.
